right.question: How is a critical fatigue area defined for aircraft control cables?
right.answer:
A critical fatigue area is defined as:  
the working length of a cable where the cable runs over, under, or around a pulley, sleeve, or through a fair-lead; any section where the cable is flexed, rubbed, or worked in any manner; or any point within 1 foot of a swaged-on fitting. [1]

right.question: How do I find broken wires in a control cable during an inspection?
right.answer: To find broken wires in a control cable during an inspection, pass a cloth over the critical fatigue areas to snag on broken wires, which will clean the cable for a visual inspection and detect broken wires if the cloth snags on the cable. Additionally, perform a very careful visual inspection since a broken wire may not protrude but may lie in the strand and remain in the helix position, potentially showing up as a hairline crack; if a broken wire of this type is suspected, further inspection with a magnifying glass of 7 power or greater is recommended [2].

right.question: When must a kinked control cable or one with a popped core be replaced?
right.answer: A kinked control cable or one with a popped core must be replaced regardless of wear or broken wires [1].

right.question: How much can the outer wires of a control cable wear before the cable has to be replaced?
right.answer: The outer wires of a control cable must not wear beyond 40 to 50 percent before the cable has to be replaced. [1]

right.question: What proof load is used to test cable terminals and splices before installation?
right.answer: 60 percent of the cable breaking strengths given in Table 7-3 and Table 7-4 [1].

right.question: What is the minimum edge distance and spacing for a single row of rivets?
right.answer: For a single row of rivets, the edge distance should not be less than 2 times the diameter of the rivet and the spacing should not be less than 3 times the diameter of the rivet. [1]

right.question: What slope is the steepest allowed for a scarf patch in a plywood skin?
right.answer: The steepest slope permitted for all kinds of plywood in a scarf patch is 1 in 12 [1].

right.question: What diameter of safety wire should I use with the double-twist method on parts with large holes?
right.answer: .032-inch diameter safety wire should be used with the double-twist method on parts that have a hole diameter larger than .045 inch [1].

right.question: After safetying a turnbuckle, how many threads of the terminal may still show?

right.question: What resistance must the electrical bond between a piece of equipment and the aircraft structure have?
right.answer: Less than 2.5 milliohms [1].

right.question: What is galvanic corrosion and how can I recognise it?
right.answer: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals make contact in the presence of an electrolyte. It is usually recognizable by the presence of a buildup of corrosion at the joint between the metals. [1]

right.question: What does exfoliation corrosion look like and where does it usually show up?
right.answer: Exfoliation corrosion shows itself by lifting up the surface grains of a metal by the force of expanding corrosion products occurring at the grain boundaries just below the surface [1]. It usually shows up on extruded sections where grain thickness is usually less than in rolled forms [1].

right.question: Why does heated titanium change colour, and should the coloured film be removed?
right.answer: Heated titanium changes colour because different oxides form on its surface at various temperature ranges: a blue oxide at 700–800 °F, a purple oxide at 800–950 °F, and a gray or black oxide at 1,000 °F or higher [1]. These coatings are protective discolorations and should not be removed [1].

right.question: Which torque values do I use for nuts and bolts when the manufacturer gives none?

right.question: What goes wrong if a vented fuel tank cap is replaced with an unvented one?
right.answer: Fuel starvation and possible collapse of the fuel tank or cell occurs. [1]

right.question: Can a metal fuel tank be welded or soldered, and what has to be done first?
right.answer: Yes, a metal fuel tank can be welded or soldered, but only if it has been adequately purged of fuel fumes [2]. First, the tank must be purged of fuel fumes [2].

right.question: How far apart can clamps be when supporting wires and cables in an aircraft?

right.question: Which gas is recommended for inflating aircraft tires, and which must never be used?
right.answer: Nitrogen is recommended for inflating aircraft tires, and oxygen must never be used. [1]

right.question: Why is it dangerous to service lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries in the same area?
right.answer: It is dangerous to service lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries in the same area because introduction of acid electrolytes into alkaline electrolyte will destroy the nickel-cadmium battery and vice-versa [1].

right.question: Which materials can be checked with magnetic particle inspection?

right.question: How reliable is a mechanical punch tester for judging the condition of aircraft fabric?
right.answer: A mechanical punch tester is not reliable for judging the condition of aircraft fabric because its accuracy depends on individual device calibration, total coating thickness, brittleness, and types of coatings and fabric. It is particularly inaccurate for glass fiber fabric, which will easily shear and indicate a very low reading regardless of the true breaking strength. Additionally, if the fabric tests in the lower breaking strength range or if overall fabric cover conditions are poor, more accurate field tests may be required [1].

right.question: How should oxygen and fuel gas cylinders be secured in a welding area?

right.question: How should a mechanic determine rivet size, spacing, and edge distance when making a sheet-metal repair?
right.answer:
A mechanic should determine rivet size, spacing, and edge distance by following these steps:

1. For single row rivets, the edge distance should not be less than 2 times the diameter of the rivet and the spacing should not be less than 3 times the diameter of the rivet [1].  
2. For double row, triple, or multiple row rivets, the edge distance and spacing should not be less than the minimums shown in Figure 4-5 [5].  
3. Rivet size should be determined based on the sheet thickness, using a rule of approximately three times the sheet thickness for rivet diameter [4].  
4. The number of rivets per inch of width is found in Table 4-10, and the total number of rivets is calculated by multiplying the number per inch by the width of the sheet [4].  
5. Rivet edge distance is defined as the distance from the center of the rivet hole to the nearest edge of the sheet, and rivet spacing is the distance from the center of the rivet hole to the center of the adjacent rivet hole [1].  
6. Unless structural deficiencies are suspected, the rivet spacing and edge distance should duplicate those of the original aircraft structure [1].  
7. If the metal skin is damaged extensively, replace an entire sheet panel and ensure the repair seams lie along stiffening members, bulkheads, etc., with rivet size, splicing, and pattern matching the original manufactured seams [2].  
8. Use the acceptable drill size for each rivet diameter as specified in MIL-HDBK-5 or MMPDS-10, and avoid drilling oversized holes that decrease effective tensile areas in highly stressed members [3].  

These guidelines ensure that the repair meets the minimum requirements for structural integrity as specified in AC 43.13-1B CHG 1.

right.question: What practices does the circular recommend for repairing corrosion damage, and when should a damaged part be replaced?
right.answer: The circular recommends that corrosion damage be repaired by removing all corrosion and corrosion products, cleaning and stripping all finish from the corroded area, removing corrosion products, and restoring the surface protective film [2]. If the corrosion damage is severe and exceeds the damage limits set by the aircraft or parts manufacturer, the part must be replaced [2]. If manufacturer information and limits are not available, a DER must be consulted before the aircraft or part is returned to service [2].

right.question: How does the circular describe selecting and installing bolts, nuts, and safety devices?
right.answer:
The circular describes selecting and installing bolts, nuts, and safety devices as follows:

- Bolts and nuts must be locked or safetyed, except self-locking nuts; do not reuse cotter pins or safety wire [1].
- Bolt holes, especially in primary connecting elements, have close tolerances; it is generally permissible to use the first-lettered drill size larger than the nominal bolt diameter, except when AN hexagon bolts are used in light-drive fit (reamed) applications [1].
- For safety wiring, when using a double-twist method, a minimum wire diameter of .032 inch should be used on parts with hole diameters larger than .045 inch; .020-inch safety wire is specified for smaller applications [2].
- When securing castellated nuts, tighten to the low side of the selected torque range, unless otherwise specified, and if necessary, continue tightening until a slot lines with the hole; safety wiring for blind tapped holes should follow general instructions; hollow-head bolts are safetied as for regular bolts [3].
- Cylinder hold-down nuts and cap screws must be tightened to recommended torque limits to prevent improper stressing and ensure even loading; installation of baffles, brackets, or other extraneous parts under nuts or cap screws is discouraged due to potential loosening risks [4].

Note: The circular does not provide a comprehensive, step-by-step procedure for selecting and installing bolts, nuts, and safety devices, but outlines specific requirements and limitations for each component and method. [1, 2, 3, 4]

right.question: What procedures does it describe for inspecting, preserving, or repairing fabric-covered aircraft surfaces?
right.answer:
The CONTEXT describes procedures for repairing fabric-covered aircraft surfaces, specifically:

- All materials used in repairs must be of a quality at least equal to the original materials, and workmanship must return the fabric to its original airworthy condition [1].
- For repairs, any combination of hand-sewn and overlapped and doped seams may be used [1].
- All pigmented dope coats (including aluminum-pigmented) must be removed to clear dope preliminary coats before installing a new fabric section or finishing tape; the old dope may be softened with appropriate dope thinner and removed by scraping with a dull-bladed knife, with sanding being optional [1].
- Dope must not run down the back side of the fabric or drip through the wing, to avoid cosmetic damage and high gloss finish [1].
- When repairing fabric other than cotton or linen approved under a manufacturer’s type certificate or STC, follow the manufacturer’s or supplier’s repair instructions [2].
- For overlapped and doped seams on wingtips, wing butts, perimeters of wing control surfaces, empennage surfaces, and fuselage areas, overlap the fabric 2 inches and cover with a finishing tape at least 3 inches wide, centered on the outside edge of the overlap seam [5].
- For overlapped and doped seams on a wing’s leading edge, on aircraft with Vne up to and including 150 mph, overlap 2 inches and cover with a finishing tape at least 3 inches wide, centered on the outside edge of the overlap seam [5].

No procedures for inspecting or preserving fabric-covered aircraft surfaces are described in the provided CONTEXT. The content focuses exclusively on repair methods and materials, not inspection or preservation. [1, 2, 5]  

Therefore, the CONTEXT does not describe procedures for inspecting, preserving, or repairing fabric-covered aircraft surfaces in a comprehensive or complete manner. It only describes repair procedures.

right.question: What guidance does it give for inspecting and repairing aircraft electrical wiring and connections?
right.answer:
Guidance for inspecting and repairing aircraft electrical wiring and connections includes:

- Inspect equipment, electrical assemblies, and wiring installations for damage, general condition, and proper functioning to ensure continued satisfactory operation of the electrical system [1].
- Wires and cables must be visually inspected for support, protection, and general condition, with support devices (clamps, grommets, etc.) at intervals of not more than 24 inches, except when in troughs, ducts, or conduits [3].
- Metal stand-offs must be used to maintain clearance between wires and structure; tape or tubing is not acceptable as an alternative [3].
- Inspect for evidence of breaks, cracks, dirt, or moisture in plastic sleeves over wire splices or terminal lugs [4].
- Splices must occur at intervals of at least 10 feet unless specifically authorized [4].
- When replacing wiring or coaxial cables, identify them properly at both equipment and power source ends [4].
- When replacing wiring, review the aircraft maintenance manual to determine if the original aircraft manufacturer has approved a substitution; if not, contact the OAM for acceptable replacement [4].
- Inspect wire annually for abrasions, defective insulation, condition of terminations, and potential corrosion [5].
- Grounding connections for power, distribution equipment, and electromagnetic shielding must be checked to ensure electrical bonding resistance has not been significantly increased by loosening or corrosion [5].
- Turn off all electrical power prior to starting an inspection or performing maintenance for personal safety and to avoid fire [3].

Note: All inspections must be conducted in conjunction with other preventive maintenance, and manufacturer’s recommended corrosion inspection programs take precedence over general guidelines [2].

right.question: What does it recommend for inspecting and repairing transparent plastic aircraft components, such as windows or windshields?
right.answer:
For inspecting and repairing transparent plastic aircraft components, such as windows or windshields, the following is recommended:

- For inspection: Clean the plastic with water and mild soap using a clean, soft, grit-free cloth, sponge, or bare hands. Do not use gasoline, alcohol, benzene, acetone, carbon tetrachloride, fire extinguisher, deicing fluids, lacquer thinners, or window cleaning sprays, as these will soften the plastic and cause crazing. Do not rub with a dry cloth, as it may cause scratches and build up electrostatic charge. If no great amount of scratching is visible after cleaning, finish with a good grade of commercial wax applied in a thin even coat and polished lightly with a soft cloth. Do not attempt hand polishing or buffing until the surface is clean, using a soft, open-type cotton or flannel buffing wheel [3].

- For repair:
  - Minor repairs: Stop-drill the ends of a crack with a #30 drill (1/8 inch) to prevent stress concentration. Drill a series of number 40 holes about half an inch from the edge of the crack, spaced about half an inch apart, and lace through with brass safety wire, then seal with clear silicone [1].
  - Temporary repairs: Stop-drill the ends of the crack, then drill number 27 holes every inch or so along the crack. Use AN515-6 screws and AN365-632 nuts with AN960-6 washers on both sides of the plastic to hold the crack together [4].
  - Permanent repairs: Stop-drill the ends of a small crack with a #30 or 1/8-inch drill. Use a hypodermic syringe and needle to fill the crack with polymerizable cement (such as PS-30 or Weld-On 40), allowing capillary action to fill it completely. Soak a 1/8-inch acrylic rod in cement, insert it into the stop-drilled hole, allow the repair to dry for about 30 minutes, and then trim the rod flush with the sheet [4].

Note: For pressurized airplanes, repairs must follow the manufacturer’s recommendation [1]. Replacement panels must use material equivalent to that originally used by the manufacturer [2].
